bib.title: Automated Unit Test Improvement using Large Language Models at Meta

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Automated Unit Test Improvement using Large Language Models at Meta. Alshahwan, Chheda, Finegenova, Gokkaya, Harman, Harper, Marginean, Sengupta, Wang. FSE '24 (arXiv:2402.09171v1, Feb 2024; Meta TestGen-LLM).

COVERAGE: about 62,000 of 72,654 chars, 12 pages. The abstract, all 8 sections, Tables 1-6, and the start of the references were read. The rest of the references were skipped as bibliography. Figure 2 is a Sankey diagram and was not extracted as an image, but the text states its numbers. No appendices exist.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: The core design is a chain of three filters, applied to LLM output before any human sees it: builds, passes on 5 repeated runs (flakiness check), then improves coverage. Whatever fails a filter is discarded. This is a verification gate that does not rely on the model's self-assessment.
  number: 5 executions
  setup: Kotlin test classes for Android at Meta. Two internal LLMs (LLM1, LLM2). Line coverage measured with Jacoco. Per-test-case filtering.
  quote: "a test that does not pass on every one of five executions is deemed flaky."
  where: p.2, Section 2
- claim: Filter yield falls at each stage in the controlled evaluation.
  number: 75% / 57% / 25%
  setup: 86 Kotlin components of Instagram Reels (55) and Stories (31). Four prompts, two LLMs. Percentages are of test classes with at least one qualifying test, per the Section 3.3 list. The abstract words it as "test cases".
  quote: "75% of test classes had at least one new test case that builds correctly." / "57% of test classes had at least one test case that builds correctly and passes reliably." / "25% of test classes had at least one test case that builds correctly, passes and increases line coverage"
  where: p.5, Section 3.3
- claim: In deployment the tool improved about 10% of the classes it was applied to, and 73% of its recommendations were accepted by engineers. The abstract says 11.5%, the body says about 10%, and the paper does not explain the gap.
  number: 196 of 1,979 classes; 73%
  setup: Three test-a-thons (Instagram Nov and Dec 2023, Facebook Dec 2023). Data collected 29 Oct to 29 Dec 2023.
  quote: "196 test classes were successfully improved, while the TestGen-LLM tool was applied to a total of 1,979 test classes. TestGen-LLM was therefore able to automatically improve approximately 10% of the test classes to which it was applied. Over all, 73% of TestGen-LLM test improvements were accepted by developers."
  where: p.6, Section 4
- claim: The 73% acceptance compares favourably with the 50% acceptance for Meta's earlier automated repair deployment.
  number: 50%
  setup: Comparison is to an earlier Meta repair deployment (ref [31]), a different task.
  quote: "it compares favorably with previous attempts to deploy automated repair at Meta (where 50% of recommended fix improvements were accepted and landed into production [31])."
  where: p.6
- claim: Per-test-case guarantees replaced class-level ones after reviewers found duplicate tests. One landed diff held four tests that were only superficially different. Measuring each test's own coverage contribution removed the duplicates.
  number: 4 duplicate tests in one diff; 8 initial diffs
  setup: Initial trial of 8 diffs in Meta's CI code review.
  quote: "one of the diffs that ultimately landed initially contained four test cases. However, all four were only superficially different."
  where: p.3, Section 3.1
- claim: Reviewers accepted most diffs even when the verified property was only a proxy. All rejections were for things the filters cannot see (no assertion, trivial getter, multiple responsibilities per test).
  number: 16 of 17 landed (Nov); 36 of 42 accepted (Dec Instagram); 144 of 280 accepted (Facebook)
  setup: Instagram Nov test-a-thon (36 engineers, 105 diffs, 16 from TestGen-LLM); the TestGen-LLM-only Instagram Dec run; Facebook Dec run.
  quote: "Of the 42 diffs: 36 were accepted by the engineer reviewing them. 4 were rejected and/or abandoned. 2 were withdrawn." / "of the 280 diffs generated by TestGen-LLM: 144 were accepted by the engineer reviewing them. 64 were rejected and/or abandoned. 61 did not receive a review. 11 were withdrawn."
  where: p.5-6, Sections 3.4 and 3.4.1
- claim: Coverage can be gamed by an assertion-free test, so a coverage filter alone misses it. A test that merely executed an unexecuted method (with a "TODO" for the assertion) passed the filter but was rejected by the human reviewer.
  number: none
  setup: Instagram Nov test-a-thon.
  quote: "The test case did extend coverage (simply by executing the previously unexecuted method-under-test), but it was rejected by the engineer reviewing the diff because it failed to contain an assertion."
  where: p.4, Section 3.2.1
- claim: Per-trial success rate is low (about 4-5%), so the pipeline is generate-many-and-filter.
  number: 831 of 23,535 (Instagram, 0.04); 490 of 8,996 (Facebook, 0.05)
  setup: Deployment trials, where a trial is one attempt to generate one test case. A trial succeeds only if the test builds, passes and adds coverage.
  quote: "Facebook 490 8,996 0.05 / Instagram 831 23,535 0.04"
  where: p.6, Table 3
- claim: Temperature had little effect, so zero was chosen as the default. The deployment-mode temperature results are confounded.
  number: about 4% at temperatures 0.0, 0.2 and 0.5 (per the text); 1,215 of 30,483 at T=0
  setup: Experimental mode on 86 components. Deployment Table 4 has very unequal sample sizes. The authors list confounders (coverage accumulates, logarithmic growth).
  quote: "all had approximately 4% success over all test cases suggested. We therefore set the default temperature to zero."
  where: p.5-7
  note: Table 4 shows per-trial rates of 0.01 at T=0.2 and 0.5, which does not match the "approximately 4%" in the text. Use with care.
- claim: An ensemble of LLMs and prompts adds unique tests, so each combination contributes something.
  number: LLM1 found 13 tests (15% of files), LLM2 found 16 (19%). Unique tests per prompt for LLM2: extend_coverage 5, statement_to_complete 2, extend_test 2, corner_cases 1.
  setup: 86 test classes, four prompts (Table 2).
  quote: "Using just LLM2, TestGen-LLM was able to find 16 tests (19% of files have at least one new test)."
  where: p.5
- claim: Generated tests were near-duplicates ("all or nothing" similarity), so a syntactic-equality filter on test bodies was added.
  number: none
  quote: "tests generated were either almost verbatim copies of others previously generated, or very different."
  where: p.7
- claim: In the first test-a-thon the tool ranked sixth by number of tests landed. Its median coverage gain per test was small.
  number: 17 tests, rank 6; median 2.5 lines; one test covered 1,326 lines; 6 of 17 tests covered 1 extra line
  setup: Instagram Nov 2023, 36 engineers.
  quote: "The median number of lines of code added by a TestGen-LLM test in the test-a-thon was 2.5."
  where: p.4
- claim: Pass rates compare favourably with other work, though models and setups differ.
  number: 57% executable (25% improving coverage), vs 29% for TeCo (Nie et al.) and about one third for ChatGPT (Yuan et al.)
  quote: "approximately approximately 57% of Kotlin test cases generated are executable (with 25% improving coverage)."
  where: p.8

LIMITS
- Authors concede that line coverage is "merely an expedient proxy for 'improvement'". Branch coverage was unavailable at their scale. They name mutation coverage as better but too costly at scale.
- Success rate per test is low, about 4-5%. Deployment results are confounded because production coverage accumulates and gets harder to extend. Samples are unbalanced, with LLM2 and T=0 dominating.
- The test-a-thon setting (heightened focus on testing, recent refactors, authors pre-screening recommendations in Dec) means "not a perfect example of diff time deployment". The first run's diffs were submitted manually, with human-added notes.
- Internal, undisclosed LLMs. The paper is an experience report with no ablation against a no-filter baseline and no bug-finding or mutation-score measure.
- The model generates tests. It does not verify its own agentic output, and the filters are deterministic scripts, not a model judge. Each test case is a fresh LLM call, with no retry or re-prompt feedback loop yet (re-prompting is listed as future work).
- The system never mutates or deletes existing tests, so no-regression holds "by construction".
- It is dated: the models are 2023 and internal, with no frontier or agentic models.
- Possible weakness for the harness note: the filters check that tests are valid and add coverage, not that they are correct (a test can encode a wrong assertion that passes).

BUILDS ON: Assured LLM-based Software Engineering ([6], the authors' own earlier work, Harman and colleagues). Genetic Improvement (ref [40]; original formulation Langdon and Harman, ref [25]). Generate-and-test automated program repair (refs [14, 15, 22, 31, 47]). Search Based Software Engineering (refs [17, 18]). Repeated-execution flaky test detection (refs [10, 28]). Test oracle problem (Barr et al., ref [7]). Meta's earlier Sapienz and diff-time deployment work (Alshahwan et al. 2018, ref [4]).

CODE: none. Table 2 holds the prompt templates. For example, extend_coverage reads: "Here is a Kotlin unit test class and the class that it tests: {existing_test_class} {class_under_test}. Write an extended version of the test class that includes additional unit tests that will increase the test coverage of the class under test." (p.6)

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): TestGen-LLM top-level architecture. LLMs feed candidate test cases through the Builds, Passes and Improves coverage filters, then onward code review in CI. Shows the filter cascade at a glance.
- Fig 2 (p.5): Sankey diagram of filter outcomes as percentages of all test cases (86 Reels and Stories components, four prompts, two LLMs). Shows the attrition at each filter.
- Tables 1 and 3-6 hold the leaderboard and success rates.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The PDF is a preprint-style ACM version with a placeholder DOI. Table 4 and the "approximately 4%" text are inconsistent (see above). The abstract's 11.5% disagrees with the text's about 10%. Layout columns in the extraction are interleaved but readable.
